title: Bad Trips Guide, Round 1
intro: This is your whole Bad Trips guide as it is published today (it matches the editor HTML you pasted, block for block), with my suggestions marked where they apply. Nothing changes until you approve it.

The first card is the one big question: how the quick version and the long version split the work. Most of the repetition is between the checklist, the Longer Triage and the long sections, so those cuts wait for your answer. The other cards are repeats and safety lines inside the long part, which come out whichever way you answer.

Pangram (your extension, on the published post) reads the guide as AI overall. The full analysis didn't open from here, so there are no window readings on this page yet. Humanizing starts once the structure is settled, so no work goes into paragraphs that are about to be cut.

structure.label: Structure
structure.about: how the quick version and the long version split the guide, and where a part goes

repeat.label: Said twice
repeat.about: a point the guide already makes elsewhere: one copy goes, the other stays

safety.label: Safety in one place
safety.about: a caution or call-for-help line said in several places, or one that changes nothing a reader does

question.label: Your call
question.about: something only you can decide or know

suggestions.title: How should the quick and long versions split the work?
suggestions.question: A (my pick): the Quick Bad Trip Checklist stays at the top, but each step becomes its heading and one or two of your own lines saying what to do, with a link to its section below. Step 1 keeps its danger signs in full, since someone in an emergency shouldn't have to click. Everything else is said once, in the long part. The Longer Triage goes: its paragraphs that aren't said anywhere else (the emergency room isn't magic; the body writing the horror story; love isn't stubbornness) move to the sections they belong to. B: keep today's order (checklist, Longer Triage, outside help, medical rescue, remedies, tripsitting, the shadow-work essays) and only cut the repeats inside it, keeping the fuller copy each time. C: take the quick version out of the post, since the web app at ibogaqueen.com/1625-2/ already is one, and open the post with a short "In a crisis right now?" box: the danger signs, the brain-damage branch and the link to the app.
suggestions.why: Most of the guide's advice is told three or four times: in the checklist (15 steps), in the Longer Triage (5 questions), and again in the long sections. The brain-damage order is told six times, "I do not yet have data that pes-caprae aborts MDMA" five times, the support lines three times, and one 38-word quote ("I hear how vast and certain this feels...") twice word for word. A quick version that only points to the long part lets each thing be said once.
suggestions.stays: Whichever you pick, each checklist step keeps its heading and its first action in your words, and every paragraph that goes is listed with the place that already says it.
suggestions.advice_note: A: it keeps the quick read you want and takes out the third and fourth tellings. B leaves most of the repetition between the checklist and the long part. C makes the post depend on the web app for the quick version. With A, the next page shows the new checklist in full, step by step, for your OK.

suggestions.title: The brain-damage order, told twice in the long part
suggestions.what: The numbered Core Order list moves up into "If Someone Says “My Brain Feels Damaged”", in place of the paragraph that says the same steps in prose ("After DMSO, the second move depends on the drug..."). The list's heading ("The Core Order When the Brain Feels Damaged") and the paragraph after it ("After medical danger, environment, dose...") go. Item 4 drops its last sentence, which the beach morning glory section says ("I do not yet have data showing that pes-caprae aborts MDMA").
suggestions.why: The section and the list give the same five steps (DMSO first, check the symptoms, pes-caprae for a psychedelic, magnesium for MDMA, medics in parallel), in two sections a few screens apart. The list is quicker to follow in a crisis and has one thing the prose doesn't (the Metta NMT sniffer). The paragraph after the list says the remedies are done ("After medical danger ... have been considered"), but the remedies come after it; "That finishes the rescue-chemistry side of the guide" already does that job at the right place.
suggestions.stays: The section keeps its reasons and evidence: why you take the report seriously, the checks, the stroke studies, and the treatment-window warning with "while someone calls medics".
suggestions.deciding: Whether you'd rather keep the prose and drop the list (then the sniffer goes into the prose).
suggestions.advice_note: Approve: the list is your clearest version, and it sits where a reader in trouble looks.
suggestions.found_by: my read; readers A and B

edits.before: After DMSO, the second move depends on the drug. With a psychedelic, a serious brain-damage feeling changes the objective from calming the trip to stopping it: I would use Ipomoea pes-caprae as the next move. With MDMA, I would move instead to magnesium chloride and the broader electrolyte branch. I do not yet have evidence that pes-caprae aborts MDMA.
The Core Order When the Brain Feels Damaged
If this is MDMA, move to magnesium chloride and the broader electrolyte branch instead. I do not yet have data that pes-caprae aborts MDMA.
edits.after: If this is MDMA, move to magnesium chloride and the broader electrolyte branch instead.

suggestions.title: When to call for help, in one section
suggestions.what: "When Peer Support Isn't Enough" moves, with its three paragraphs (when to get urgent help; "I might kill someone to test this theory"; local emergency services, 988 and 911), from the tripsitting part up into "When to Bring In Outside Help", as its third part, under its own heading at the same level as the other two. The mental-health list's first item ("The person may be unsafe to themselves or others.") goes, since the moved paragraph says it with the details. The line under the medics list ("The remedies below can begin while help is being arranged...") goes, since the next section opens with the same point ("An emergency means act now...").
suggestions.why: Today the guide lists when to call for help in about seven places (checklist steps 1 and 9, the Longer Triage, the two lists here, When Peer Support Isn't Enough, and the harm section). You asked for the safety lines in one spot: this puts the medics list, the mental-health list and the urgent-help paragraph together where a reader looks for them.
suggestions.stays: The danger signs in checklist step 1, and the call-for-help lines inside each emergency (the seizure's five minutes, the chest-pain line, serotonin syndrome, the harm script), stay where the reader acts on them.
suggestions.deciding: Whether the tripsitting part should keep a one-line pointer to this section where the heading was.

suggestions.stays: The hierarchy's first sentence stays: it is for acute situations, not merely uncomfortable trips.

suggestions.title: Why the hierarchy comes first, said a third time
suggestions.what: "The hierarchy appears before the mystical sections because love doesn’t require us to ignore the body..." (the whole paragraph) goes.
suggestions.why: The two paragraphs before it make the point (not every crisis is emotional; a gut or brain problem belongs in a different branch), and "Every hard experience is not a profound lesson..." in Why Bad Trips Tend to Happen says its last two lines.
suggestions.stays: "Psychedelic culture often treats every crisis as emotional or spiritual..." and the paragraph after it.
suggestions.deciding: Whether "A gut-driven mental hell is not automatically shadow work" is a line you want to keep somewhere.

edits.before: The hierarchy appears before the mystical sections because love doesn’t require us to ignore the body. Medical danger may need medical help while field rescue begins. A bad room gets fixed. A gut-driven mental hell is not automatically shadow work. A dose or combination problem does not need to become a spiritual curriculum.

suggestions.why: Actual Activated Charcoal, a few sections up, says both: it can help gut toxicity, it adsorbs drugs and can reduce a trip, and you use zeolite when you want to keep the trip.
suggestions.stays: The charcoal-water section keeps its first line ("...different from zeolite and from swallowing charcoal") and goes straight on to "What I usually use is the water portion".

suggestions.title: Movement, in the menu again
suggestions.what: Two items go from the Grounding Menu's Body list ("Try two minutes of safe movement: ..." and "Then ask whether movement made you clearer or more impulsive..."), and two from its Ordinary world list ("Do one ordinary task you can clearly finish when the body wants movement." and "Pace along a clear contained path when pacing helps.").
suggestions.why: Stillness or Movement? says the two-minute test and its question, pacing in a contained space, and the small task with an endpoint; Alone at 3 a.m. lists the movements (pacing, stretching, a few slow wall push-ups).
suggestions.stays: The Body list keeps feet, hands on heart and belly, something with weight, unclenching. Ordinary world keeps food, walking with a sober person, going outside safely, and the strenuous-exercise warning.
suggestions.deciding: "Shaking out the arms and legs" is said only here and in checklist step 4; if step 4 shrinks too, say if you want it kept somewhere.

suggestions.title: Humic acid: lick it first, or smell it first?
suggestions.question: The Core Order's first step says "Smell humic acid, take a 5mg lick of it", and Humic Acid Brings Brain to Optimal Function says a 5mg lick sends your brain "into hyperfunctionality". Some Remedies Require More Caution says eating it "can produce a hyperintelligent state", could destabilize somebody prone to mania, "I wouldn’t use it casually during a bad trip", and "I’d start with" smelling it. Which should the guide say for someone whose brain feels damaged: (a) smell it, and lick a tiny bit only if smelling doesn't help and they aren't prone to mania; (b) smell it and lick 5mg, as the Core Order says; (c) your words?
suggestions.why: A reader who follows the Core Order would do what the caution section warns against.
suggestions.stays: All three passages stay as they are until you answer.
suggestions.advice_note: (a): it fits both passages, and the lick stays available when smelling isn't enough.

suggestions.stays: Everything stays where it is until you answer.
suggestions.advice_note: (a): someone opening the guide in trouble needs the checklist first, and the greeting opens the half they read once they are safe.
